items.label: Customers can place and pay for an order
Restaurant receives the order in the merchant app
Push notification when the order is out for delivery

task.explanation: Ordering and order receipt are Musts (no product without them); delivery notifications are a Should; favourites a Could; recommendations are an explicit Won't for this release.

prompt: A client sent their MoSCoW list for a 10-week build. Mark the lines that misuse MoSCoW.

task.prompt: A client sent their MoSCoW list for a 10-week build. Mark the lines that misuse MoSCoW.

segments.text: Must: users can sign up and log in.
Must: admin can export reports to PDF, Excel, CSV and Google Sheets.
segments.issue: Four export formats are unlikely all to be essential for launch; probably one Must and the rest Should or Could.
A cosmetic preference is rarely essential to launch.

segments.text: Must: everything else in the backlog.
segments.issue: If everything is a Must, nothing is prioritised; MoSCoW needs real Shoulds and Coulds as a contingency.

prompt: A common MoSCoW guideline is that Must items take no more than about 60% of the available effort, leaving Should and Could as contingency. Check this release plan.

task.prompt: A common MoSCoW guideline is that Must items take no more than about 60% of the available effort, leaving Should and Could as contingency. Check this release plan.

fields.label: Must as a share of capacity
Points of Must work above the 60% guideline

task.explanation: Must = 84 / 120 = 70%, which is 12 points over the 72-point guideline. The plan also exceeds capacity by 20 points, so some Coulds (and probably Shoulds) will not fit.

prompt: Two weeks before launch the team is behind. The plan has 3 Must stories left (13 points), 2 Should stories (8 points) and 2 Could stories (5 points). Remaining capacity is 18 points.

task.prompt: Two weeks before launch the team is behind. The plan has 3 Must stories left (13 points), 2 Should stories (8 points) and 2 Could stories (5 points). Remaining capacity is 18 points.

steps.question: What do you drop first?
options: One Must story
The Could stories
The Should stories
Nothing; ask the team to work weekends
steps.explanation: Coulds exist precisely to be dropped when time runs short.

steps.question: After dropping the Coulds, 21 points remain against 18 points of capacity. What next?
options: Drop a Must story
Agree with the client which Should moves to the next release
Quietly reduce testing
Re-estimate the Musts lower
steps.explanation: Musts protect the launch. Moving a Should is a client decision that the PM should bring with the numbers.

prompt: Put these steps for running a MoSCoW session with a client in order.

task.prompt: Put these steps for running a MoSCoW session with a client in order.

items.label: Agree the release goal and the fixed constraint (date or budget)
Agree what Must means: the release fails without it
Sort each item, challenging every Must
Check Musts fit within about 60% of capacity
Record the Won'ts in the scope document and share

task.explanation: Definitions and the goal come before sorting; capacity checks the result; Won'ts are written down so they are not re-litigated.

prompt: The client's CEO joins a sprint review and says a new chatbot feature "is a Must" for the release that ships in three weeks. The team is already at capacity.

task.prompt: The client's CEO joins a sprint review and says a new chatbot feature "is a Must" for the release that ships in three weeks. The team is already at capacity.

steps.question: What is your first response?
options: Accept it as a Must and add it to the sprint
Refuse because the scope is signed
Ask what fails at launch without it, to test whether it meets the agreed meaning of Must
Tell the CEO the team will work overtime
steps.explanation: Testing against the agreed definition keeps MoSCoW honest without dismissing the CEO.

steps.question: It really is essential for a partner launch. What now?
options: Add it and hope velocity rises
Drop testing on other features
Show what must leave the release to make room, or what date or budget change is needed, and let the client choose
Swap it in for the lowest-priority Must without telling anyone
steps.explanation: A new Must displaces something. Present the trade explicitly and record the decision.

prompt: What does a Won't item mean in MoSCoW?

options: It is agreed as out of scope for this release, though it may come later
It will never be built
It is a low-priority item the team will do if time allows
It was rejected by the developers
mcq.explanation: Won't means "won't have this time". Recording it manages expectations for the current release without closing the door.

prompt: Why does MoSCoW work best with a fixed date or fixed budget?

options: Because it estimates effort automatically
The fixed constraint forces real trade-offs, so Should and Could items act as contingency
Because clients prefer fixed dates
Because it removes the need for a backlog
mcq.explanation: Without a fixed constraint, everything can drift into Must. A timebox makes the categories meaningful.

prompt: A client marks 90% of the backlog as Must. What is the most useful thing to do?

options: Accept it; the client knows their business
Re-label some items yourself
Switch to a different framework without discussion
Revisit the definition of Must against the launch goal and ask which items the launch truly fails without
mcq.explanation: MoSCoW only helps when Musts are scarce. Re-anchoring on the definition is the usual fix.
